practicalQuestion: How should carbohydrate, fluid, sodium, and recovery intake be organized across a same-day lift and field-practice schedule when the goal is to support both sessions without creating unnecessary gastrointestinal burden?

decisionContext.sport: Strength session followed later by field practice
decisionContext.outcome: Preserve training quality and between-session recovery
decisionContext.constraints: Four to six hours between sessions; campus dining options; variable sweat loss and gastrointestinal tolerance

evidenceConfidence.rationale: The library has relevant expert guidance on feeding between sessions less than 8 hr apart, on sodium and fluid replacement, and on reducing gastrointestinal discomfort. It also has field data showing fluid deficits carry over between same-day practices. No source tests a lift followed by field practice in collegiate athletes. The main feeding targets come from a narrative review in young professional male rugby league players and an elite soccer consensus statement. They are starting ranges, not tested protocols, so any direction must stay conditional.

dimensions.sourceReview: Every claim is checked against original source text. The sources are a narrative review (rugby league), a consensus statement (elite soccer), a systematic review and meta-analysis, three observational field studies in American football, and a two-player case study.
dimensions.directness: Indirect to moderate. The between-session feeding guidance addresses recovery windows under 8 hr but was not tested on a lift-then-field day. The hydration carryover data come from two-a-day football practices, which are closer to this context.
dimensions.consistency: Directionally consistent: refuel carbohydrate early and repeatedly, replace fluid and sodium, and individualize. Daily carbohydrate targets differ between sources (up to 8 g/kg/day versus 8 to 10 g/kg/day for intense multi-session training).
dimensions.transferability: Populations are mostly male: young professional rugby league players, elite soccer players, endurance-trained and recreationally active males, high school and collegiate American football players, and two Australian Football players. No source includes female collegiate athletes.

bottomLine.text: No library source tests a same-day lift followed by field practice in collegiate athletes. Expert reviews from professional rugby league and elite soccer, plus field hydration studies in American football, support a coordinated plan. Start carbohydrate and protein soon after the lift. Keep carbohydrate coming through the 4 to 6 hour gap. Replace measured fluid losses with sodium-containing fluids and food. Use multiple carbohydrate types and familiar foods to limit gastrointestinal burden.

recommendedDirection.text: If the lift precedes practice by 4 to 6 hours and both sessions matter, consider a staged plan. First, an early post-lift feed of carbohydrate (about 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg) with protein. Second, continued carbohydrate either hourly or every 2 hr. Third, fluid and sodium replacement sized to each athlete's measured body mass loss. Fourth, multiple-transportable carbohydrate and familiar foods for athletes with gastrointestinal complaints. Treat all amounts as starting ranges to adjust individually, because they come from professional male rugby league and elite soccer guidance rather than tested collegiate two-session protocols.

actions.title: Feed early after the lift
actions.text: The rugby league review describes an initial feed of 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg carbohydrate within 1 hr after training and encourages protein within 1 hr after a resistance session. The UEFA statement suggests 20 to 25 g of high-quality protein at 3 to 4 hour intervals, which would place one protein feeding in a 4 to 6 hour gap. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): combine the carbohydrate and protein in one post-lift meal or snack.

actions.title: Spread carbohydrate across the gap
actions.text: For recovery under 8 hr, the review lists two options. One is 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg per hour for the first 4 hr. The other is 0.6 to 1.0 g/kg every 2 hr after the initial feed. A cited study found that carbohydrate taken every 30 min during recovery improved performance 4 hr later, with highly variable responses. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with only 4 to 6 hr available, the hourly option fills most of the gap. Athletes prone to gastrointestinal upset may tolerate smaller, more frequent amounts better than a large meal close to practice.

actions.title: Choose foods that limit gastrointestinal burden
actions.text: The review links multiple-transportable carbohydrate to less upper abdominal discomfort. It suggests appealing options such as fruits and juices, cereal bars, and milk drinks to encourage intake. The UEFA statement describes training the gut by taking carbohydrate during exercise to improve tolerance. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): build a campus dining or grab-and-go plate from these foods, and trial any new during-practice fueling on a lower-stakes day first.

actions.title: Replace fluid and sodium based on measured loss
actions.text: The rugby league review lists 1.25 to 1.5 L of fluid per kg of body mass lost, combined with food, as soon as practically possible. For example, a 1 kg loss implies 1.25 to 1.5 L. It states sodium in recovery fluids should equal or exceed sweat sodium (20 to 80 mmol/L), which is somewhat higher than typical commercial sports drinks. Field data show fluid deficits carry over after two-a-day practices. Poor rehydration may also increase glycogen use in the next session.

actions.title: Set the day's total carbohydrate to the training load
actions.text: Daily targets differ by source. The UEFA statement uses a sliding scale of 3 to 8 g/kg/day based on the training scenario. The rugby league review lists 8 to 10 g/kg/day for intense training of 1 to 2 sessions daily. Collegiate American football players in one study ate low amounts of carbohydrate. The UEFA statement notes that the order of gym and field sessions can affect habitual macronutrient intake. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): check that breakfast and the evening meal also carry enough carbohydrate, so the between-session plan is not doing all the work.

monitoring.label: Body mass change per session
monitoring.text: Sweat rates in American football are cited at about 0.5 to 4 L per hour. One study found fluid balance ranged from a 2.35% loss to a 0.47% gain among athletes in the same practices. Weighing before and after the lift and the practice gives the body mass loss that the 1.25 to 1.5 L/kg replacement guidance requires.

monitoring.label: Do not rely on urine alone
monitoring.text: In high school football players, urine color and urine specific gravity did not significantly detect body mass change. The authors state that no single hydration measure is without limitations. Pair urine checks with body mass.

monitoring.label: Gastrointestinal tolerance and actual intake
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): briefly log what each athlete ate and drank between sessions and any gut symptoms during practice. The cited evidence supports multiple-transportable carbohydrate and gut training for tolerance, and shows collegiate players may under-eat carbohydrate.

guardrails.text: Amounts in this brief are starting ranges from professional male rugby league and elite soccer guidance. They are not individual prescriptions. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): athletes with gastrointestinal conditions, heat illness history, weight goals, or disordered eating concerns need individual planning with sports dietitian and medical staff.
Sweat losses vary widely between athletes in the same session, and the cited sodium target exceeds typical sports drinks. Do not apply one fixed fluid or sodium amount to the whole team.

limitations.text: The feeding timing and amount guidance comes from a narrative review for young professional male rugby league players and an elite soccer consensus statement. Neither tests a lift-then-field-practice day in collegiate athletes.
The rehydration and glycogen link comes from a meta-analysis of 18 studies published from 1976 to 2017, half in endurance-trained males, not team-sport athletes.
Hydration field data come from male high school and male American football players during outdoor practices. No source includes female athletes.
The performance and gastrointestinal benefits of recovery carbohydrate come from a cited study summarized in a review, with a standard deviation about as large as the mean effect.

whatCouldChange.text: Trials in collegiate team-sport athletes comparing between-session feeding plans on a lift-then-field day, with training quality and gastrointestinal outcomes, could confirm or narrow these ranges.
Sweat rate and sweat sodium testing in this squad could show whether the 20 to 80 mmol/L sodium target and fluid volumes need adjusting.
Data in female collegiate athletes could change the transferability of these hydration findings.

evidenceTension.text: Daily carbohydrate targets differ. The UEFA consensus uses a sliding scale of 3 to 8 g/kg/day by training scenario, while the rugby league review lists 8 to 10 g/kg/day for intense training of 1 to 2 sessions daily. Collegiate American football players in one observational study ate low carbohydrate. The gap between sources does not change the direction to refuel between sessions. It does mean the daily total should be set to the actual training load rather than taken from either source alone.

assumptions: The strength session comes first and field practice follows 4 to 6 hours later, as stated.
Both sessions are moderate to high intensity; session duration and environmental heat were not specified.
The squad may include both male and female athletes; sex was not specified.
Staff can weigh athletes before and after sessions to estimate fluid losses.
coverageGaps: No study of nutrition timing on a same-day strength session followed by field practice in collegiate team-sport athletes.
No trial measuring gastrointestinal symptoms with different between-session feeding plans in team-sport athletes.
No sweat sodium data for collegiate team-sport athletes to anchor individual sodium targets.
No data in female collegiate team-sport athletes on between-session fueling or hydration.
No evidence on how campus dining access or meal timing affects between-session intake.
